roles: replacement for Judas among the Twelve

events.title: Chosen by lot to replace Judas
events.summary: After Peter argues from the Psalms that Judas's office must be filled, two men who had followed Jesus from John's baptism to the ascension are put forward, Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias. The group prays and casts lots; the lot falls on Matthias, who is counted with the eleven.

summary: Matthias was chosen by lot to restore the Twelve after the death of Judas Iscariot. He had accompanied Jesus throughout his public ministry and was a witness of the resurrection. He is never mentioned again in the New Testament.
textSays: Acts says only that he had been with the disciples from the baptism of John until the ascension, that he was one of two candidates, and that the lot fell on him so that he was numbered with the eleven apostles.

interpretations.view: Honored as a full apostle and saint; the choice is read as showing that the apostolic office continues by succession. Feast on 14 May (Roman) and 9 August (Eastern).

A minority (notably G. Campbell Morgan) suggested the apostles acted prematurely and that Paul was God's real choice; most Protestant commentators reject this, since Luke presents the choice without criticism and the Twelve function as a group afterwards (Acts 6:2).

traditions.text: Eusebius reports that Matthias was one of the seventy disciples sent out by Jesus.

Accounts of his later mission and death conflict: some place his preaching in Cappadocia or by the Caspian Sea (Colchis), others say he was stoned in Jerusalem. His relics are claimed by the Abbey of St. Matthias in Trier, said to have been brought by Empress Helena.
traditions.source: Later hagiography (Greek and Latin martyrologies); locators need verification

voice: Quiet and steady, a witness rather than a preacher; speaks of what he saw with Jesus from the Jordan to the Mount of Olives without claiming more.

alternatives.label: Late date, just before Paul's conversion on later chronologies

gifts.name: Full of the Spirit and wisdom

events.title: Chosen as one of the Seven
events.summary: When Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked in the daily food distribution, the apostles asked the community to choose seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom. Stephen is named first and described as full of faith and the Holy Spirit; the apostles pray and lay hands on the seven.

events.title: Works wonders and signs
events.summary: Luke says Stephen, full of grace and power, did great wonders and signs among the people. His role quickly goes beyond serving tables.

events.title: Dispute with the Synagogue of the Freedmen
events.summary: Members of a synagogue of Freedmen, with Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia, argue with Stephen but cannot withstand the wisdom and Spirit with which he speaks. Cilicia was Saul's home province.

events.title: Arrested on charges of speaking against temple and law
events.summary: Opponents stir up the people and produce witnesses who say Stephen claimed Jesus would destroy the temple and change the customs of Moses. Luke calls the witnesses false; the council sees his face like the face of an angel.

events.title: Speech before the council
events.summary: The longest speech in Acts retells Israel's story from Abraham through Joseph, Moses, the tabernacle and Solomon's temple. Its themes: God met his people outside the land; Israel repeatedly rejected the deliverers God sent; the Most High does not dwell in houses made with hands. It ends by accusing his hearers of resisting the Spirit and betraying the Righteous One.

events.title: Vision of the Son of Man standing
events.summary: Gazing into heaven, Stephen sees the glory of God and Jesus standing at God's right hand, and says so aloud. It is the only place outside the Gospels where someone other than Jesus uses the title Son of Man.

events.title: Stoned outside the city
events.summary: The crowd drags him out and stones him. The witnesses lay their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen commits his spirit to the Lord Jesus and prays that this sin not be held against them, echoing Jesus's words on the cross.

events.title: Burial and the scattering
events.summary: Devout men bury and mourn him. A great persecution follows, the believers scatter through Judea and Samaria, and some go as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, where Greeks first hear the gospel.

events.title: Remembered by Paul
events.summary: Recounting his conversion, Paul recalls that he stood by approving and guarding the garments when the blood of Stephen, Christ's witness, was shed.

summary:
Stephen was one of seven men appointed to oversee the daily distribution of food in the Jerusalem church, but Acts portrays him above all as a Spirit-filled preacher and worker of signs. A Greek-speaking Jew, he provoked opposition among Hellenistic synagogues in Jerusalem, was charged with speaking against the temple and the law, and delivered a long speech before the Sanhedrin that retold Israel's history as a story of God's presence beyond the temple and the people's resistance to his messengers.

He was stoned to death, praying for his killers and committing his spirit to Jesus in words that mirror Luke's account of the crucifixion. His death is a hinge in Acts: it introduces Saul of Tarsus, triggers the persecution that scatters the church beyond Jerusalem, and sets in motion the mission to Samaria and the Gentiles.

The church has honored him since antiquity as the protomartyr, the first to die for Christ, and his speech remains one of the most studied texts in Acts for what it says about the temple, the law and early Christian readings of Israel's scriptures.
textSays: Acts names Stephen first among the Seven and says he was full of faith, the Spirit, grace and power, performed wonders and signs, and out-argued opponents from several diaspora synagogues. False witnesses accused him of saying Jesus would destroy the temple and change Mosaic customs. He gave a long speech (Acts 7), saw Jesus standing at God's right hand, and was stoned while Saul watched approvingly. The text does not call him a deacon; the noun is not used of the Seven, though the related verb (to serve tables) is.

interpretations.view: Venerated as the protomartyr and archdeacon, the model for the diaconate as an ordained order. Feast on 26 December (West) and 27 December (East). His prayer for his persecutors is often linked to Paul's later conversion.

Stephen is read as a model of faithful witness and as a preacher who grasped early that the coming of Christ relativized the temple. Many see the Seven as prototypes of deacons while noting the text does not use the title.

Many scholars see in the Hebrews and Hellenists of Acts 6 a real division in the Jerusalem church, with Stephen's circle holding a more critical stance toward the temple, which explains why they, not the apostles, were driven out (Acts 8:1). Whether the speech preserves Stephen's own views or Luke's composition is debated; Luke does label the anti-temple charges false, which complicates the reading of Stephen as anti-temple.

The speech's charge that Israel always resisted the Spirit has been used polemically in later Christian history. Many modern interpreters, Jewish and Christian, stress that it stands within the prophetic tradition of internal critique (compare Neh 9:26) spoken by a Jew to Jews, not as a condemnation of a whole people.

failures: The text records none; some read his closing accusation as deliberately provocative
turningPoints: Vision of the standing Son of Man
Death, which sets the church's mission moving outward

context: Jerusalem had many synagogues for Jews returned from the diaspora, including freed slaves and their descendants. Greek-speaking Jewish believers (Hellenists) and Aramaic-speaking believers (Hebrews) formed distinct groups in the earliest church. Under Roman rule the Sanhedrin normally lacked authority to carry out executions (compare John 18:31), so Stephen's death may have been a mob action or may reflect a period of weak Roman oversight; this is debated.
legacy: Stephen became the archetype of the Christian martyr, and his feast follows Christmas in most calendars. Augustine's *City of God* 22.8 describes healings associated with relics of Stephen after their reported discovery near Jerusalem in 415. His speech shaped Christian reflection on the temple, and his death is the backdrop for Paul's conversion.

traditions.text: In 415 a priest named Lucian reported finding Stephen's remains at Caphar Gamala near Jerusalem after a dream; the relics were distributed widely and miracles were reported in North Africa.
traditions.source: Augustine, City of God 22.8; Lucian's letter on the discovery (locator needs verification)

traditions.text: Tradition places his stoning outside the northern gate of Jerusalem, later called St. Stephen's Gate (the name has also attached to the eastern Lions' Gate).
traditions.source: Byzantine pilgrim tradition; Empress Eudocia built a basilica north of the city in the 5th century

voice: Fluent, learned and urgent, a Greek-speaking Jew who argues from the whole sweep of Israel's history; calm under threat and willing to say hard things to the powerful.

events.title: Chosen as one of the Seven
events.summary: Named second after Stephen among the seven appointed to oversee the food distribution.

events.title: Preaches Christ in Samaria
events.summary: Scattered by the persecution, Philip preaches in a city of Samaria; crowds respond to his signs, many are baptized, including Simon the magician.

events.title: Baptizes the Ethiopian official
events.summary: Sent by an angel to the desert road to Gaza, Philip hears an Ethiopian court official reading Isaiah 53, explains the passage as being about Jesus, and baptizes him.

events.title: Preaches along the coast to Caesarea
events.summary: Philip appears at Azotus (Ashdod) and evangelizes the coastal towns until he reaches Caesarea.

events.title: Hosts Paul at Caesarea
events.summary: About twenty years later Paul's party stays at Philip's house in Caesarea. Luke notes that Philip had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.

journey.note: Preaches and baptizes in a Samaritan city
On the desert road toward Gaza meets the Ethiopian
Settles in Caesarea; later hosts Paul

summary: Philip was one of the Seven chosen in Jerusalem and became the church's first named cross-cultural evangelist. After Stephen's death he took the gospel to Samaria, then baptized an Ethiopian official on the road to Gaza, and worked his way up the coast to Caesarea, where he was still living when Paul visited two decades later. Acts calls him the evangelist to distinguish him from Philip the apostle, with whom later tradition often confused him.
textSays: He was one of the Seven; he preached and worked signs in Samaria; he was directed by an angel and the Spirit to the Ethiopian; he was snatched away by the Spirit and found at Azotus; he lived in Caesarea and had four virgin daughters who prophesied.

interpretations.view: Venerated as a deacon and evangelist (in the East also as bishop of Tralles); feast 6 June (West) and 11 October (East).
Held up as the model lay evangelist who crosses ethnic and religious boundaries (Samaritans, a eunuch from Africa) in fulfillment of Acts 1:8.

traditions.text: Polycrates of Ephesus and Papias place a Philip and his prophesying daughters at Hierapolis in Asia; Eusebius appears to merge Philip the apostle and Philip the evangelist in reporting this.

voice: Warm, mobile and practical; asks simple questions (Do you understand what you are reading?) and goes wherever he is sent.

alternatives.label: Earlier estimate (he is a young man at Stephen's death and calls himself aged in Phlm 1:9)
Executed at the end of the two-year house arrest of Acts 28
Later in Nero's reign after release and a second imprisonment (Eusebius/Jerome tradition)
alternatives.source: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.22; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 5

nation: Diaspora Jew; Roman citizen; citizen of Tarsus

skills.name: Pharisaic training in the law under Gamaliel
Use of Roman citizenship and legal process

events.title: Approves of Stephen's death and persecutes the church
events.summary: Introduced as a young man guarding the garments of those stoning Stephen, Saul then goes house to house dragging believers to prison. Paul later describes himself as having violently persecuted the church of God out of zeal.

events.title: Encounter with the risen Jesus near Damascus
events.summary: Travelling with letters from the high priest, Saul is struck by a light, hears Jesus ask why he is persecuting him, is blinded, and is baptized by Ananias three days later. Acts tells the story three times; Paul's letters describe it as God revealing his Son in him and calling him to the Gentiles.

events.title: Arabia, Damascus and escape over the wall
events.summary: Paul goes to Arabia (the Nabatean kingdom) and returns to Damascus, where he preaches in the synagogues. When the governor under King Aretas guards the city, he is let down through a window in the wall in a basket.

events.title: First visit to Jerusalem; sent home to Tarsus
events.summary: Three years after his conversion he spends fifteen days with Cephas and meets James. Barnabas vouches for him; when Hellenist Jews try to kill him, believers send him via Caesarea to Tarsus, where he spends several years in Syria and Cilicia.

events.title: Teacher at Antioch and famine relief
events.summary: Barnabas fetches Saul to Antioch, where they teach for a year and the disciples are first called Christians. They carry famine relief to the elders in Judea.

events.title: First missionary journey
events.summary: Sent out by the Antioch church with Barnabas, Paul preaches in Cyprus (where he is first called Paul), Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. He is stoned at Lystra and left for dead, then returns through the same towns appointing elders.

events.title: Council in Jerusalem
events.summary: Paul and Barnabas argue that Gentile believers need not be circumcised. The apostles and elders, with James giving the decision, agree, asking Gentiles to avoid a few practices offensive to Jews. Galatians 2 records a private meeting where the pillars extend the right hand of fellowship; whether it is the same meeting as Acts 15 or the famine visit is debated.

events.title: Confronts Peter at Antioch
events.summary: When Peter withdraws from eating with Gentiles under pressure from men from James, Paul opposes him to his face for not walking in step with the truth of the gospel.

events.title: Second missionary journey into Europe
events.summary: After parting from Barnabas over John Mark, Paul takes Silas, adds Timothy, and after a vision of a man of Macedonia crosses to Europe. He founds churches at Philippi (where he and Silas are beaten and jailed), Thessalonica and Berea, speaks at the Areopagus in Athens, and stays eighteen months in Corinth, where he appears before the proconsul Gallio.

events.title: Third journey and long ministry in Ephesus
events.summary: Paul spends two to three years in Ephesus teaching daily in the hall of Tyrannus, until a riot of silversmiths devoted to Artemis. He revisits Macedonia and Greece, collects money for the Jerusalem poor, raises Eutychus at Troas and bids farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus.

events.title: Arrest in the temple and imprisonment at Caesarea
events.summary: Accused of bringing a Gentile into the temple, Paul is seized by a mob and rescued by Roman soldiers. After a plot against his life he is moved to Caesarea, held two years under Felix, and, facing transfer to Jerusalem under Festus, appeals to Caesar. He defends himself before Agrippa II.

events.title: Shipwreck and arrival in Rome
events.summary: Sailing late in the season, the ship is caught by a northeaster, drifts fourteen days and is wrecked on Malta. Paul reaches Rome in spring and lives two years under guard in rented quarters, preaching the kingdom of God without hindrance. Acts ends there.

summary:
Paul, also called Saul, was a Pharisee from Tarsus who persecuted the earliest followers of Jesus and then, after an encounter with the risen Christ near Damascus, became the most influential missionary and theologian of the first generation of the church. A Roman citizen at home in both Jewish and Greek worlds, he spent some three decades founding communities of Jews and Gentiles across Asia Minor, Macedonia and Greece, supporting himself by tentmaking and staying in touch with his churches through letters.

Thirteen New Testament letters bear his name. Seven are accepted by virtually all scholars (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon); the authorship of the others is debated. These letters, the earliest Christian writings we have, argue that in Jesus's death and resurrection God has fulfilled his promises to Israel and opened his people to the nations, so that Gentiles belong by faith and the Spirit without becoming Jews through circumcision. Acts devotes more than half its length to him and narrates three missionary journeys, his arrest in Jerusalem, two years in custody at Caesarea and a perilous voyage to Rome.

Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome. Early Christian tradition, beginning with 1 Clement, holds that he was executed there under Nero. His reading of the gospel has shaped every major theological movement in the West, from Augustine to Luther to the New Perspective, and remains contested between traditions.
textSays: Paul calls himself a Hebrew of Hebrews from the tribe of Benjamin, circumcised on the eighth day, a Pharisee, blameless under the law, and a former persecutor (Phil 3:5-6). Acts adds that he was born in Tarsus, a Roman citizen from birth, raised in Jerusalem under Gamaliel, and a tentmaker. He says he saw the risen Lord and was called as apostle to the Gentiles (Gal 1:15-16; 1 Cor 15:8). He lists beatings, three shipwrecks, a stoning, hunger and danger (2 Cor 11:23-28), and a thorn in the flesh he asked to have removed (2 Cor 12:7-9). He hoped to visit Rome and go on to Spain (Rom 15:24). Acts ends with him preaching in Rome under guard; no biblical text records his death, though 2 Tim 4:6-8 presents him as expecting it.

interpretations.view: Paul is the great apostle alongside Peter; together they are the founders of the Roman church, sharing a feast on 29 June. Justification is read as God's making the sinner truly righteous through grace received in baptism and lived out in faith working through love (Gal 5:6). Paul's letters are read within the tradition and teaching office of the church.

Paul is honored as equal of the apostles and read through the Greek Fathers, especially John Chrysostom. Emphasis falls on union with Christ, participation in his death and resurrection, and theosis, with justification one facet of salvation rather than its organizing center.

Paul's letters, especially Romans and Galatians, are the clearest statement of the gospel: sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ's righteousness imputed to them, apart from works of the law. Luther's and Calvin's commentaries made this the hinge of the Reformation.

interpretations.tradition: New Perspective on Paul (E. P. Sanders, J. D. G. Dunn, N. T. Wright)
interpretations.view: Second Temple Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation but of covenantal grace. Paul's critique of works of the law targets markers that separated Jews from Gentiles (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath); his main concern is that Jews and Gentiles form one family in Christ. Critics respond that Paul also opposes human achievement in general (Rom 4:4-5); defenders reply that they do not deny this, only that it is not the main front.

interpretations.tradition: Paul within Judaism (e.g. Pamela Eisenbaum, Mark Nanos, Paula Fredriksen)
interpretations.view: Paul never left Judaism; he remained a law-observant Jew whose mission was to bring Gentiles to Israel's God without making them Jews. Critics answer that passages like Phil 3:7-8 and 1 Cor 9:20-21 show a more radical relativizing of the law; proponents read these as statements about status, not abandonment of practice.

strengths: Theological depth and pastoral warmth in letters
Supported himself so as not to burden churches
failures: Violent persecution of the church before conversion, which he never minimized (1 Cor 15:9)
Sharp break with Barnabas over John Mark
turningPoints: Arrest in the temple and appeal to Caesar

context: Tarsus was a major Hellenistic city and center of Stoic learning. Diaspora Jews like Paul's family could hold Roman citizenship, which gave legal protections (no flogging without trial, appeal to Caesar). Paul travelled Roman roads and shipping lanes and normally began in synagogues, where God-fearing Gentiles provided a bridge. The date of his ministry is anchored by the Gallio inscription at Delphi, which places Gallio's proconsulship of Achaia in about 51-52. Authorship of Ephesians, Colossians and 2 Thessalonians is debated, and most critical scholars regard 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus as written in his name after his death; traditional scholars defend Pauline authorship of all thirteen, often appealing to the use of secretaries (Rom 16:22) and to a release and second imprisonment.
legacy: Paul's letters became the core of the New Testament epistolary canon and were already being collected and called hard to understand by the time of 2 Pet 3:15-16. Marcion in the 2nd century made Paul his sole apostle; Irenaeus and others answered by reading him with the other apostles. Augustine's reading of Romans shaped Western theology of grace; Luther's and Calvin's shaped Protestantism; Karl Barth's Romans commentary (1919) launched 20th-century neo-orthodoxy. His missionary method shaped modern missions.

traditions.text: Paul preached in east and west, taught righteousness to the whole world, reached the limit of the west, and bore witness before rulers before departing the world.

Paul was beheaded in Rome under Nero, on the same occasion as or near the time of Peter's death; Eusebius cites Gaius of Rome on the trophies (tombs) of the apostles on the Vatican hill and the Ostian Way, and Dionysius of Corinth on their martyrdom.
After defending himself, Paul was released and went on preaching before a second Roman imprisonment and death.
Paul died by beheading, like John the Baptist.
He was a short man, bald, bow-legged, with eyebrows meeting and a somewhat hooked nose, full of grace.
traditions.source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 3 (2nd century; locator needs verification)

traditions.text: His execution took place at Aquae Salviae (Tre Fontane) on the Ostian Way, and he was buried where the Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls now stands.
traditions.source: Later Roman tradition (site tradition needs verification)

voice: Intense, argumentative and affectionate by turns; thinks aloud in rapid questions and answers (What then shall we say?), quotes Scripture constantly, boasts only in weakness, and calls his converts his children.
