alternatives.label: Latest point he is known alive (1 Cor 9:6); later date unknown

roles: mentor to Paul and John Mark

events.title: Sells a field and gives the proceeds
events.summary: Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus whom the apostles call Barnabas, sells land and lays the money at the apostles' feet. Luke sets him as the positive example before the story of Ananias and Sapphira.

events.title: Vouches for the converted Saul
events.summary: When the Jerusalem disciples fear Saul, Barnabas takes him to the apostles and tells how he had seen the Lord and preached boldly in Damascus.

events.title: Sent to Antioch; fetches Saul
events.summary: The Jerusalem church sends him to investigate the mixed church at Antioch. He rejoices at what he sees, exhorts them, then goes to Tarsus to find Saul. They teach together for a year; there the disciples are first called Christians.

events.title: Famine relief to Judea
events.summary: After Agabus predicts famine, the Antioch disciples send relief to the elders in Judea by Barnabas and Saul, who return with John Mark.

events.title: Set apart for the first mission
events.summary: Listed first among Antioch's prophets and teachers, Barnabas is set apart with Saul by the Holy Spirit and sent out, first to his home island of Cyprus.

events.title: Hailed as Zeus at Lystra
events.summary: After a lame man is healed the crowd calls Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and a priest prepares sacrifice. The two tear their clothes and insist they are human.

events.title: Defends Gentile freedom at the Jerusalem council
events.summary: With Paul he reports God's signs among the Gentiles; the council's letter calls them beloved men who risked their lives. James, Cephas and John give them the right hand of fellowship.

events.title: Carried away at Antioch
events.summary: When Peter withdraws from table fellowship with Gentiles, Paul says that even Barnabas was carried away by the hypocrisy.

events.title: Sharp disagreement with Paul over Mark
events.summary: Barnabas wants to take his cousin John Mark again; Paul refuses because Mark had left them in Pamphylia. The disagreement is sharp, and Barnabas sails with Mark to Cyprus. Acts does not mention him again.

events.title: Still remembered as a working apostle
events.summary: Writing to Corinth, Paul names Barnabas alongside himself as an apostle who works for a living rather than accepting support, suggesting continued respect.

journey.note: Home island; a Levite of Cypriot birth
Sails with Mark after parting from Paul

summary:
Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus named Joseph, was one of the most trusted leaders of the early Jerusalem church. The apostles nicknamed him Son of Encouragement, and Acts shows him living up to it: he gave the proceeds of a field to the community, vouched for Saul when others were afraid of him, and was sent to Antioch to examine the new Jewish-Gentile church, where he rejoiced, encouraged it and brought Saul in to teach.

With Paul he led the first mission from Antioch through Cyprus and southern Asia Minor, and with Paul he argued at the Jerusalem council that Gentile believers should not be required to be circumcised. Luke calls both men apostles (Acts 14:14). Early on Barnabas is named first, then the order shifts to Paul and Barnabas as Paul becomes the main speaker.

Their partnership ended over whether to give John Mark, Barnabas's cousin, a second chance. Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus and disappears from Acts, but Paul later speaks of him with respect and later reconciles with Mark, suggesting Barnabas's patience was vindicated.
textSays: Acts calls him a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith (Acts 11:24), a Levite of Cypriot birth, a prophet and teacher, and an apostle. Paul says he was carried away by Peter's withdrawal from Gentiles at Antioch (Gal 2:13) and that he worked for his living (1 Cor 9:6). Col 4:10 identifies Mark as his cousin.

interpretations.view: Honored as an apostle (though not of the Twelve) and founder of the Church of Cyprus, whose autocephaly was confirmed in 488 after the reported discovery of his relics. Feast 11 June.

Commonly held up as a model of encouragement and mentoring: he saw potential in Saul and in Mark when others did not. The split with Paul is often read as a case where both men acted in good faith and God used the result to double the mission.

Some see in Gal 2:13 a more serious rupture between Paul and Barnabas over table fellowship than Acts's account of a personal dispute about Mark; others think Luke and Paul are describing different aspects of the same strained relationship.

strengths: Willingness to step back as Paul grew
failures: Swayed by the withdrawal from Gentile table fellowship (Gal 2:13)

context: Cyprus had a substantial Jewish community. As a Levite owning land, Barnabas illustrates that the old restriction on Levitical land ownership was no longer strictly observed in the diaspora. Antioch, the third city of the Roman empire, became under his leadership the base for the Gentile mission.
legacy: An early Christian writing, the *Epistle of Barnabas* (c. 100-130), was attributed to him by Clement of Alexandria, though modern scholars regard it as pseudonymous. Tertullian attributed the Letter to the Hebrews to him. Cyprus regards him as its founder and patron.

traditions.text: Barnabas was stoned to death at Salamis in Cyprus by Jews opposed to his preaching, and Mark buried him.
traditions.source: Acts of Barnabas (5th century; locator needs verification)

traditions.text: His tomb was revealed near Salamis in 488 with a copy of Matthew's Gospel on his chest, strengthening Cyprus's claim to independence from Antioch.
Barnabas wrote the Letter to the Hebrews.
He was one of the seventy disciples sent out by Jesus.
traditions.source: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 2.20, cited in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 1.12.1 (locator needs verification)

voice: Generous, steady and kind; speaks up for people others are wary of, prefers to encourage before correcting, and does not mind letting someone else do the talking.

names.original: Silas (Greek form of an Aramaic name); Silvanus (Latin)
names.meaning: Possibly from Aramaic sh'ila, asked; Silvanus: of the forest

events.title: Carries the council's letter to Antioch
events.summary: Chosen as a leading man among the brothers, he and Judas Barsabbas deliver the Jerusalem decision and, as prophets, encourage the believers.

events.title: Chosen as Paul's partner
events.summary: After the split with Barnabas, Paul takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia.

events.title: Beaten and jailed at Philippi
events.summary: He and Paul are flogged and put in stocks; at midnight they pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens the doors, and the jailer believes. Both are revealed to be Roman citizens.

events.title: Mission in Thessalonica, Berea and Corinth
events.summary: He stays behind in Berea with Timothy, rejoins Paul in Corinth and preaches there. Paul later names him among those who proclaimed Christ to the Corinthians.

events.title: Named as co-sender and helper
events.summary: Silvanus is co-sender of both Thessalonian letters. 1 Peter says it was written through Silvanus, a faithful brother, which may mean he was the secretary or the bearer.

journey.note: A leader in the Jerusalem church

summary: Silas was a prophet and respected leader in the Jerusalem church who was sent to Antioch with the council's decision and then chose to travel with Paul on the second missionary journey. Like Paul a Roman citizen, he shared the beating and imprisonment at Philippi and helped found the churches of Thessalonica, Berea and Corinth. In the letters he appears under his Latin name Silvanus as co-sender of 1 and 2 Thessalonians, and 1 Peter says it was written through him, which links him to both Paul and Peter.
textSays: Acts calls him a leading man among the brothers and a prophet; Paul and Peter call him Silvanus. Most scholars identify Silas and Silvanus as one person, since they share Paul's company in the same places at the same time.

interpretations.view: Counted among the seventy disciples in Eastern lists and honored as a saint; feast 13 July (West) and 30 July (East).

Some argue that writing through Silvanus means he drafted the letter, which would explain its polished Greek; others argue the Greek phrase usually means the letter carrier (as in Ignatius's letters) and so says nothing about composition.

traditions.text: Later Eastern tradition makes Silas bishop of Corinth.
traditions.source: Pseudo-Dorotheus lists of the seventy (needs verification)

voice: Steady and musical, a man who sings in prison; an authoritative Jerusalem voice who can reassure Gentile churches that the mother church stands with them.

alternatives.label: Younger estimate based on his youth in 1 Tim 4:12

nation: Son of a Jewish mother and Greek father, from Lystra
roles: leader of the church at Ephesus

gifts.name: A gift given through prophecy and the laying on of hands

events.title: Joins Paul at Lystra
events.summary: A well-regarded disciple whose mother was a Jewish believer and father a Greek, Timothy is chosen by Paul, who circumcises him because of the Jews in the area who knew his father was Greek.

events.title: Faith learned from grandmother and mother
events.summary: Paul recalls the sincere faith that lived first in Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and that he had known the sacred writings from childhood.

events.title: Founding work in Macedonia and Achaia
events.summary: He stays with Silas in Berea, then rejoins Paul and helps in Corinth.

events.title: Sent back to strengthen the Thessalonians
events.summary: Paul, unable to bear the uncertainty, sends Timothy from Athens to establish the persecuted church; he returns with good news of their faith and love.

events.title: Envoy to Corinth
events.summary: Paul sends his beloved and faithful child in the Lord to remind the Corinthians of his ways, and asks them to make sure he has nothing to fear among them.

events.title: Travels with the collection
events.summary: He is among the delegates accompanying Paul toward Jerusalem and sends greetings in Romans as Paul's fellow worker.

events.title: With Paul in prison
events.summary: Co-sender of Philippians, Colossians and Philemon. Paul says he has no one else like him, who will genuinely care for the Philippians' welfare, and that he served with Paul like a son with a father.

events.title: Left in charge at Ephesus
events.summary: 1 Timothy has Paul urging him to stay in Ephesus to stop certain people teaching different doctrine, and tells him not to let anyone despise his youth.

events.title: Summoned to Paul before his death
events.summary: 2 Timothy asks him to come quickly before winter, bringing Mark, a cloak left at Troas, and the books and parchments.

events.title: Released from prison
events.summary: Hebrews reports that our brother Timothy has been set free, the only hint that he too was imprisoned.

journey.note: With Paul during the Ephesian ministry
With Paul when Romans is written
Goes ahead and waits at Troas

summary:
Timothy was Paul's closest and longest-serving co-worker. Raised in Lystra by a Jewish mother and grandmother who taught him the Scriptures, with a Greek father, he joined Paul on the second missionary journey and stayed with him for the rest of Paul's life. Paul called him his beloved child in the faith and said he had no one else like him.

Timothy served as Paul's envoy to troubled churches, strengthening the Thessalonians under persecution, representing Paul in Corinth and being promised to the Philippians. He is co-sender of six of Paul's letters. Two letters are addressed to him, portraying him as a relatively young leader in Ephesus charged with confronting false teachers and ordering church life.

His circumcision by Paul (Acts 16:3) has long puzzled readers, since Paul refused to have Titus circumcised (Gal 2:3); most explain the difference by Timothy's Jewish mother, which made him Jewish in the eyes of local synagogues.
textSays: Acts calls him a disciple well spoken of by the believers at Lystra and Iconium, son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father. The letters name his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, describe him as Paul's child and fellow worker, speak of a gift given through prophecy and laying on of hands, urge him not to let others despise his youth, mention frequent ailments for which he should take a little wine (1 Tim 5:23), and suggest timidity (1 Cor 16:10; 2 Tim 1:7).

interpretations.view: Honored as the first bishop of Ephesus and a martyr. The Pastoral Letters addressed to him are read as foundational for the ordained ministry and the transmission of apostolic teaching. Feast 26 January (with Titus, Roman calendar) and 22 January (East).

Timothy is a model of a second-generation leader formed by family faith and mentoring. Those who accept Pauline authorship of the Pastorals see real snapshots of Timothy's ministry; many critical Protestant scholars see the Pastorals as later writings that use Timothy as an ideal figure of the faithful successor.

Some scholars doubt the historicity of Timothy's circumcision in Acts 16:3, given Paul's own statements against circumcising Gentiles; others note that matrilineal descent may already have been the norm and that Paul's principle in 1 Cor 9:20 fits the account.

failures: Possibly timid or easily intimidated (1 Cor 16:10-11; 2 Tim 1:7)

context: Mixed marriages between Jews and Gentiles were uncommon but known in the diaspora. Lystra was a Roman colony in Lycaonia. The Pastoral Letters' authorship and date are debated, which affects how much of Timothy's later life can be reconstructed.
legacy: The two letters bearing his name have shaped church order, ordination and pastoral theology across traditions. Timothy has become the type of the young minister mentored by an older one.

traditions.text: Timothy was the first bishop appointed to the church at Ephesus.
He was beaten to death by a crowd at Ephesus after opposing a pagan festival procession, around the end of the 1st century.
traditions.source: Acts of Timothy (5th century; needs verification)

traditions.text: His relics were moved to the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople in 356.

voice: Earnest, gentle and loyal; a little reserved and unsure of his authority, but speaks with conviction when he talks about the Scriptures his mother and grandmother taught him and about Paul.

skills.name: Reconciler in a tense church situation

events.title: Test case at Jerusalem
events.summary: Paul brings the uncircumcised Greek Titus to Jerusalem; he is not compelled to be circumcised, which Paul presents as a defense of the gospel's freedom.

events.title: Carries out the reconciliation with Corinth
events.summary: Paul, anxious when he cannot find Titus at Troas, goes to Macedonia, where Titus arrives with news that the Corinthians have repented, which comforts Paul.

events.title: Organizes the collection
events.summary: Paul sends Titus back to complete the gift for Jerusalem, calling him his partner and fellow worker.

events.title: Left in Crete to appoint elders
events.summary: The letter to Titus says Paul left him in Crete to put things in order and appoint elders in every town, then to join Paul at Nicopolis.

events.title: Goes to Dalmatia
events.summary: 2 Timothy notes that Titus has gone to Dalmatia.

summary: Titus was a Gentile convert and one of Paul's most capable co-workers. Paul took him uncircumcised to Jerusalem as a living test of Gentile freedom, and later relied on him for the most delicate assignment of his ministry: restoring relations with the Corinthian church and completing the collection for Jerusalem. The letter addressed to him places him in Crete organizing churches and appointing elders. Oddly, Acts never mentions him; some have suggested he was Luke's brother, which would explain the silence, but that is speculation.
textSays: Paul calls him a Greek, his true child in a common faith, partner and fellow worker. He brought Paul comfort in Macedonia and showed affection for the Corinthians. The letter to Titus places him in Crete; 2 Timothy places him in Dalmatia.

interpretations.view: Honored as first bishop of Crete; feast 26 January (with Timothy) in the West and 25 August in the East.
Seen as a model of a reliable Gentile leader; the letter to Titus is read as a short manual for elders and Christian conduct, with debate over its authorship as with the other Pastorals.

traditions.text: Titus was appointed bishop of the churches in Crete.
He died in old age in Crete; his head was later venerated at Gortyn and is now kept at Heraklion.

voice: Firm, capable and diplomatic; a Greek who knows what it is to be the outsider and who can deliver hard messages without losing people's affection.

names.original: Loukas (Greek, short form of Latin Lucanus or Lucius)

alternatives.label: Tradition gives his age at death as 84; with an earlier birth the year falls earlier

nation: Probably Gentile (debated); tradition: Syrian of Antioch

events.title: Writes an orderly account for Theophilus
events.summary: The author of the Third Gospel says many had compiled narratives from eyewitnesses and that he, having followed everything carefully from the start, decided to write an orderly account so Theophilus might know the certainty of what he had been taught.

events.title: We-passage begins at Troas
events.summary: After Paul's vision of the Macedonian, Acts suddenly shifts to we: we sought to go into Macedonia. The narrator is present at Lydia's conversion in Philippi. Tradition reads this as Luke joining Paul.

events.title: Rejoins Paul from Philippi to Jerusalem
events.summary: The we-narrative resumes at Philippi and follows the voyage via Troas, Miletus, Tyre and Caesarea to Jerusalem, where we went in with Paul to James.

events.title: Voyage and shipwreck with Paul
events.summary: The most detailed sea narrative in ancient literature, told in the first person, follows Paul from Caesarea through storm and shipwreck on Malta to Rome.

events.title: With Paul in Roman custody
events.summary: Paul sends greetings from Luke the beloved physician and lists Luke among his fellow workers.

events.title: Only Luke is with me
events.summary: In 2 Timothy, with others gone or deserted, Paul says only Luke is with him.

events.title: Writes the Acts of the Apostles
events.summary: The second volume, again addressed to Theophilus, picks up from the ascension and follows the church from Jerusalem to Rome.

journey.note: Present at the founding of the church; we-passage stops here
Goes in with Paul to James
And so we came to Rome

summary:
Luke is named three times in Paul's letters, as the beloved physician, a fellow worker, and the one companion who stayed with Paul at the end. From the 2nd century on, the church has unanimously identified him as the author of the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles, which together make up more than a quarter of the New Testament, more than any other single author.

The two volumes are addressed to Theophilus and present themselves as careful research based on eyewitness tradition. The sudden switch to we in parts of Acts (the we-passages) has traditionally been read as Luke's own travel diary, placing him with Paul from Troas to Philippi, from Philippi to Jerusalem, and on the voyage to Rome. Luke's writing shows special interest in prayer, the Holy Spirit, women, the poor, Samaritans and Gentiles, and in the orderly spread of the gospel from Jerusalem to Rome.

Whether the author really was Paul's companion is debated: some critical scholars point to differences between Acts and Paul's letters, while others find the we-passages and the early, uniform attribution persuasive.
textSays: Paul calls Luke the beloved physician (Col 4:14), a fellow worker (Phlm 1:24), and says only Luke is with him (2 Tim 4:11). Neither the Gospel nor Acts names its author. In Col 4:10-14 Paul lists the only Jewish co-workers (those of the circumcision) before naming Luke, which many read as implying Luke was a Gentile.

interpretations.view: Luke is the evangelist and author of Acts, a companion of Paul who also drew on Mary's testimony for the infancy narratives. Orthodox tradition honors him as the first icon-painter. Feast 18 October.

The unanimous early attribution, the we-passages and the medical-sounding vocabulary noted by W. K. Hobart (1882, much criticized since) are taken to confirm Luke's authorship and the high historical value of Acts.

Many scholars hold that Luke-Acts was written c. 80-90 by an educated Gentile or God-fearer, possibly but not certainly Paul's companion. Differences with Paul's letters (e.g. the number of Jerusalem visits, Paul's view of the law) and the possibility that the we-style is a literary device are cited. Defenders answer that companions need not agree on everything and that a literary we would be unusual in ancient historiography without a claim to presence.

strengths: Loyalty to Paul to the end
Skill as a storyteller and historian
turningPoints: Staying with Paul when others left

context: Physicians in the Roman world were often educated slaves or freedmen. Ancient historians like Thucydides and Polybius valued eyewitness inquiry, a standard Luke's preface echoes. Luke's dating is debated: an early date (c. 62) is argued from Acts ending before Paul's trial; a later date (c. 80-90) from Luke's use of Mark and apparent knowledge of Jerusalem's fall (Luke 21:20).
legacy: Luke gave the church the Christmas story of the shepherds and the manger, the parables of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son, the Magnificat, Benedictus and Nunc Dimittis, the ascension and Pentecost narratives, and the only account of the church's first generation. He is patron saint of physicians and artists.

traditions.text: Luke, the follower of Paul, set down in a book the gospel Paul preached.
Luke was a physician whom Paul took with him, who wrote the Gospel in his own name though he had not seen the Lord in the flesh.
Luke was by birth an Antiochene and a physician who spent much time with Paul.
Luke served the Lord without distraction, had neither wife nor children, and died at 84 in Boeotia, full of the Holy Spirit.
traditions.source: Anti-Marcionite Prologue to Luke (date debated; needs verification)

traditions.text: Luke painted icons of the Virgin Mary.

voice: Measured, observant and precise, the voice of a careful researcher and physician; tells stories well, notices outsiders, and prefers to keep himself in the background.

names.meaning: John: the LORD is gracious; Marcus: Roman name

roles: author of the Gospel of Mark (traditional)

events.title: Mother's house is a meeting place
events.summary: When Peter is freed from prison he goes to the house of Mary, mother of John called Mark, where many are praying.

events.title: Joins Barnabas and Saul, then turns back
events.summary: He goes to Antioch and serves as assistant on the first journey, but leaves at Perga and returns to Jerusalem.

events.title: Cause of the Paul-Barnabas split
events.summary: Paul refuses to take him again; Barnabas, his cousin (Col 4:10), takes him to Cyprus.

events.title: Reconciled with Paul
events.summary: Later Paul lists Mark as a fellow worker and asks Timothy to bring him, because he is useful for ministry.

events.title: With Peter in Babylon
events.summary: 1 Peter sends greetings from Mark my son, from the church in Babylon, commonly understood as a code name for Rome.

summary: John Mark was a young Jerusalem believer whose mother's house was a gathering place for the church. He set out with his cousin Barnabas and Paul on the first missionary journey but turned back at Perga, which led Paul to refuse him on the next journey and caused the break between Paul and Barnabas. He later regained Paul's trust and appears with both Paul and Peter in Rome. Early tradition, beginning with Papias, identifies him as Peter's interpreter and the author of the Gospel of Mark.
textSays: Acts names him John called Mark and son of Mary of Jerusalem; Colossians calls him Barnabas's cousin; 1 Peter calls him my son. Whether all New Testament references to Mark are the same person is assumed by most but not certain.

interpretations.view: Mark is the Evangelist, interpreter of Peter, founder and first bishop of the church of Alexandria, and martyr. Feast 25 April.
Revered as the founder of the Coptic Church; the Coptic pope is reckoned his successor.

Many accept that a Mark wrote the Gospel, given the unlikelihood of attributing it to a minor figure without reason, but debate whether he was John Mark and how direct Peter's influence was. The young man who fled naked in Mark 14:51-52 is sometimes identified with Mark himself, a speculative but old suggestion.

traditions.text: Mark, having become Peter's interpreter, wrote down accurately, though not in order, what he remembered of the Lord's sayings and deeds.
traditions.source: Papias, quoted in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39.15

traditions.text: Mark was the first sent to Egypt to preach the Gospel he had written and founded churches in Alexandria.
His relics were taken from Alexandria to Venice in 828, where St. Mark's Basilica was built to house them.

voice: Quick, vivid and direct, fond of the word immediately; a man who once quit and knows what it is to be given a second chance.

names.meaning: Woman of Lydia (a region of Asia Minor)

events.title: Baptized at the riverside prayer place
events.summary: A worshipper of God from Thyatira and a dealer in purple goods, Lydia listens to Paul by the river outside Philippi; the Lord opens her heart, she and her household are baptized, and she persuades the missionaries to stay at her house.

events.title: Her house becomes the church's base
events.summary: After their release from prison Paul and Silas go to Lydia's house, see the brothers and encourage them.

summary: Lydia was a businesswoman from Thyatira trading in purple dye or cloth, and a Gentile worshipper of Israel's God. She became the first named convert in Europe when Paul preached at a riverside place of prayer in Philippi, and she opened her home as the base of the new church.
textSays: Acts says she was a seller of purple goods from Thyatira, worshipped God, had a household that was baptized with her, and hosted Paul's team and the believers. No husband is mentioned.

interpretations.view: Honored as a saint (in the East as Equal-to-the-Apostles); feast 3 August (West, varies) or 20 May (East).

Debate whether she was a wealthy merchant or a freedwoman in a smelly, low-status dyeing trade; either way she headed her own household, which shows women's leadership in Paul's churches. Some suggest Lydia is an ethnic nickname (the Lydian woman), which Thyatira's location in Lydia supports.

voice: Practical, decisive and hospitable; a trader who knows her own mind and does not take no for an answer when she invites someone home.

skills.name: Teaching and explaining the way of God

gifts.name: Hospitality and leadership of a house church

events.title: Expelled from Rome under Claudius
events.summary: Priscilla and her husband Aquila have recently come from Italy because Claudius ordered all Jews to leave Rome.

events.title: Takes Paul in at Corinth
events.summary: Paul stays and works with them because they share the trade of tentmaking.

events.title: Moves with Paul to Ephesus
events.summary: They sail with Paul and remain in Ephesus while he travels on. Here Priscilla is named before her husband.

events.title: Explains the way of God to Apollos
events.summary: When the eloquent Apollos, knowing only John's baptism, speaks boldly in the synagogue, Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately.

events.title: Church meets in their house at Ephesus
events.summary: Paul sends greetings to Corinth from Aquila and Prisca together with the church in their house.

events.title: Risked their necks for Paul; back in Rome
events.summary: Paul greets Prisca and Aquila first in Romans, calling them fellow workers who risked their necks for his life, to whom all the Gentile churches give thanks, and greets the church in their house.

events.title: Greeted in Paul's last letter
events.summary: 2 Timothy sends greetings to Prisca and Aquila, apparently back in Ephesus.

journey.note: Living in Rome until Claudius's expulsion

summary:
Priscilla, called Prisca by Paul, was with her husband Aquila one of the most important missionary couples of the early church. Expelled from Rome when Claudius ordered Jews out of the city, they settled in Corinth, where Paul lived and worked with them as a fellow tentmaker. They then moved to Ephesus ahead of Paul's long ministry there, and later returned to Rome. In each city a church met in their home.

The couple are mentioned six times, always together, and in four of the six Priscilla is named first, which was unusual in the ancient world and suggests she was the more prominent of the two in the church or of higher social rank. Acts records that both of them took the gifted preacher Apollos aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately, one of the few New Testament scenes of a woman teaching a man about doctrine.

Paul says they risked their necks for him and that all the churches of the Gentiles were grateful to them. Their mobility, trade and household leadership make them a window into how the gospel spread through ordinary work and homes.
textSays: Priscilla and Aquila are always mentioned together. Priscilla is named first in Acts 18:18, Acts 18:26, Rom 16:3 and 2 Tim 4:19; Aquila first in Acts 18:2 and 1 Cor 16:19. Acts says Aquila was a Jew from Pontus; Priscilla's origin is not stated. Both explained the way of God to Apollos. Paul calls them fellow workers in Christ Jesus.

interpretations.view: Priscilla's precedence and her role in teaching Apollos show that women taught and led in the apostolic church; this is weighed against texts such as 1 Tim 2:12 to argue those restrictions were local or situational.

Priscilla is honored as a gifted teacher, but her instruction of Apollos was private, alongside her husband, and in their home, not an exercise of authoritative church office; this is held to be consistent with 1 Tim 2:12. Egalitarians reply that the text does not mark the setting as private versus public in a way that bears on office.

Venerated with Aquila as saints and martyrs; feast 8 July (West) and 13 February (East). Roman tradition links her to the Catacomb of Priscilla and the church of Santa Prisca on the Aventine, though these probably refer to other women of the name.

Her name being placed first is usually explained either by higher social status (perhaps freeborn or of a noble Roman family) or by greater prominence in ministry. Adolf von Harnack (1900) proposed her as the author of Hebrews; the suggestion is speculative and has few followers, partly because Heb 11:32 uses a masculine participle of the author.

strengths: Generosity in opening her home in three cities

context: Suetonius (*Claudius* 25.4) reports that Claudius expelled Jews from Rome because of disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, often taken as a garbled reference to disputes over Christ; Orosius dates it to Claudius's ninth year, AD 49. Tentmakers worked with leather and cloth, and their portable trade let them move between cities. House churches were the normal form of Christian gathering for the first three centuries.
legacy: Priscilla is one of the most frequently cited figures in modern discussions of women in ministry and a model of a couple sharing work, home and mission.

traditions.text: John Chrysostom, preaching on Romans, praised Priscilla and noted that Paul named her before her husband because of her greater zeal.
traditions.source: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Romans 30 (locator needs verification)

traditions.text: Priscilla and Aquila were martyred together, in Rome or Asia Minor.

voice: Confident, gracious and clear; a working woman who is used to running a household church and can correct a brilliant preacher over dinner without crushing him.

events.title: Leaves Rome under Claudius's edict
events.summary: A Jew born in Pontus, he arrives in Corinth with Priscilla after Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome.

events.title: Works with Paul in Corinth
events.summary: Paul lodges and works with the couple as a fellow tentmaker.

events.title: Instructs Apollos in Ephesus
events.summary: With Priscilla he takes Apollos aside and explains the way of God more accurately.

events.title: Hosts churches in Ephesus and Rome
events.summary: Paul greets the church in their house in both cities and says they risked their necks for him.

summary: Aquila was a Jewish tentmaker from Pontus on the Black Sea who, with his wife Priscilla, became Paul's co-worker and host. Expelled from Rome under Claudius, the couple worked alongside Paul in Corinth, moved to Ephesus, taught Apollos, and later returned to Rome, with churches meeting in their homes. He never appears without Priscilla.
textSays: Acts calls him a Jew, a native of Pontus, and a tentmaker. He is always mentioned with Priscilla, and Paul calls them both fellow workers who risked their lives for him.

interpretations.view: Venerated with Priscilla; Eastern lists count him among the seventy and make him a bishop (sometimes of Heraclea).
Seen with Priscilla as a model of bivocational, home-based ministry.

voice: Plain-spoken and hardworking, a craftsman more at home with an awl than a lectern, who lets his wife take the lead when it comes to talking.

skills.name: Eloquence and command of the Scriptures

events.title: Preaches in Ephesus knowing only John's baptism
events.summary: An eloquent Jew from Alexandria, mighty in the Scriptures, he teaches accurately about Jesus but knows only the baptism of John.

events.title: Taught by Priscilla and Aquila
events.summary: The couple take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately.

events.title: Strengthens believers in Achaia
events.summary: With letters of recommendation he goes to Achaia, helps those who had believed through grace and powerfully refutes the Jews in public, showing from the Scriptures that the Christ is Jesus.

events.title: Becomes a party name in Corinth
events.summary: Some Corinthians say I follow Apollos against others who follow Paul. Paul answers that both are only servants: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.

events.title: Declines to return to Corinth for now
events.summary: Paul strongly urged him to visit Corinth, but he was not willing at that time. Later Titus is asked to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way.

summary: Apollos was a learned and eloquent Jew from Alexandria who preached about Jesus with great energy but knew only John's baptism until Priscilla and Aquila instructed him further. He then became a powerful teacher in Corinth, so admired that some there rallied around his name against Paul's. Paul treats him as a colleague, not a rival, and urges him to return to Corinth; his reluctance may reflect a wish not to feed the factions.
textSays: Acts describes him as an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures, instructed in the way of the Lord, fervent in spirit, teaching accurately about Jesus though knowing only John's baptism. Paul names him as a fellow servant in 1 Corinthians and expresses no criticism of him.

interpretations.view: Martin Luther suggested Apollos as the author of Hebrews because of his Alexandrian learning and skill with Scripture; many scholars have found the idea attractive, though there is no ancient testimony for it.

Some see behind the Corinthian factions a contrast between Apollos's rhetorical, perhaps Philonic, Alexandrian style and Paul's deliberately plain preaching (1 Cor 2:1-5); others caution that Paul blames the Corinthians, not Apollos.
Counted among the seventy in Eastern lists and honored as a saint; traditions make him bishop of various places (Corinth, Smyrna, Caesarea).

voice: Eloquent, learned and fervent, quick with scriptural argument in the Alexandrian style, yet humble enough to be corrected by tentmakers.

alternatives.label: Hegesippus places his martyrdom just before Vespasian's siege of Jerusalem

roles: author of the Letter of James (traditional)

skills.name: Use of Scripture to settle disputes

events.title: Named among Jesus's brothers
events.summary: The people of Nazareth list James first among Jesus's brothers, with Joses (Joseph), Judas and Simon, and mention sisters.

events.title: Does not believe in Jesus during his ministry
events.summary: John says that not even his brothers believed in him; Mark records his family trying to restrain him.

events.title: The risen Jesus appears to him
events.summary: In the early creed Paul passes on, Christ appeared to James, then to all the apostles. Many see this as the turning point that made James a believer.

events.title: With the disciples before Pentecost
events.summary: Jesus's brothers are in the upper room praying with the apostles and Mary.

events.title: Meets Paul
events.summary: On Paul's first visit the only apostle besides Cephas he sees is James the Lord's brother.

events.title: Recognized as a pillar
events.summary: Escaping prison, Peter tells the believers to report to James. James, Cephas and John, reputed pillars, give Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship.

events.title: Gives the decision at the Jerusalem council
events.summary: Citing Amos on the rebuilding of David's tent so that the nations may seek the Lord, James judges that Gentile converts should not be troubled with circumcision but should abstain from things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, what is strangled and blood.

events.title: Men from James at Antioch
events.summary: Peter withdraws from eating with Gentiles when certain men came from James; how far James himself endorsed their stance is debated.

events.title: Receives Paul and the collection
events.summary: James and the elders praise God for Paul's report but warn that thousands of law-zealous Jewish believers have heard he teaches Jews to abandon Moses, and advise him to sponsor a temple vow to show otherwise.

events.title: Stoned in Jerusalem
events.summary: Not narrated in Scripture. Josephus reports that in the interval between the procurators Festus and Albinus, the high priest Ananus convened the Sanhedrin and had James, the brother of Jesus called Christ, stoned; fair-minded citizens protested and Ananus was deposed.

summary:
James was the eldest-named of Jesus's brothers. The Gospels indicate that he did not believe in Jesus during his ministry, but Paul records that the risen Christ appeared to him, and within a few years he had become the leading figure in the Jerusalem church. Paul names him with Peter and John as one of the pillars, and Acts shows him giving the decisive judgment at the council that freed Gentile believers from circumcision.

James represented the Jewish-Christian wing of the church, devoted to the law and respected even by non-Christian Jews for his piety, hence his nickname the Just. He sought to hold together Jewish believers zealous for the law and Paul's Gentile mission, an uneasy task reflected in the tension of Gal 2:12 and Acts 21:20-25. The Letter of James, with its emphasis on practical righteousness and faith shown in works, is traditionally attributed to him.

The Jewish historian Josephus records that he was stoned on the orders of the high priest Ananus in AD 62, one of the few events in the New Testament church independently attested by a non-Christian source.
textSays: The Gospels call him one of Jesus's brothers (adelphoi). John 7:5 says the brothers did not believe in him. Paul calls him the Lord's brother, says the risen Christ appeared to him, and names him as a pillar. Acts shows him leading the Jerusalem church and speaking for it. The Letter of James is from James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and Jude introduces himself as the brother of James. The New Testament does not record his death.

interpretations.tradition: Helvidian view (most Protestants and many modern scholars)
interpretations.view: James was a son of Joseph and Mary born after Jesus, so a full younger brother (half-brother in terms of Jesus's virginal conception). Adelphos most naturally means brother, and Matt 1:25 and Luke 2:7 (firstborn) are read as consistent with later children. Critics object that adelphos can cover wider kin; supporters reply that the Gospels consistently pair the brothers with Mary.

James was a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage, so an older stepbrother of Jesus, preserving Mary's perpetual virginity. This is attested early in the *Protevangelium of James* (2nd century) and defended by Epiphanius. Supporters note Jesus entrusted Mary to John at the cross (John 19:26-27), which would be odd if she had other sons; critics regard the earlier marriage as unattested in Scripture.

James was a cousin of Jesus, son of another Mary (Mark 15:40) and perhaps identical with James son of Alphaeus. Jerome argued this in *Against Helvidius* (c. 383), noting that Hebrew and Aramaic had no separate word for cousin. Critics observe that the New Testament has a Greek word for cousin (anepsios, Col 4:10) and that Paul distinguishes the Lord's brother from the Twelve; supporters answer that Semitic usage shaped Gospel Greek.

Luther famously called the Letter of James an epistle of straw relative to the chief books (1522 preface), because it seemed to contradict Paul on justification by faith; he later softened his language. Most Protestant interpreters now read James 2 and Romans 3-4 as complementary: Paul attacks works as a basis for acceptance, James attacks a faith that produces no works.

strengths: Wise mediator between Jewish and Gentile believers
failures: Association with those whose pressure caused Peter's withdrawal at Antioch (Gal 2:12)

context: Jerusalem in the 40s-60s was tense with nationalist zeal, rising violence and conflict between the priestly aristocracy and the people. Jewish believers continued to worship at the temple. James's death in 62 came during the gap between Roman governors, when the high priest could act without Roman restraint. The James ossuary (published 2002), inscribed James son of Joseph brother of Jesus, has been the subject of a forgery trial in Israel (acquittal in 2012 for lack of proof); scholars remain divided on whether the last part of the inscription is ancient.
legacy: James became the symbol of Jewish Christianity; later Jewish-Christian groups such as the Ebionites revered him, and the Pseudo-Clementine writings exalt him above Peter. The Letter of James shaped Christian ethics on wealth, speech and care for the poor. Eastern liturgy preserves a Divine Liturgy of St. James associated with Jerusalem.

traditions.text: Ananus the high priest assembled the Sanhedrin and brought before them the brother of Jesus called Christ, James by name, with some others, and had them stoned.

James was holy from birth, drank no wine, did not cut his hair, prayed so much in the temple that his knees became hard like a camel's, was thrown from the temple pinnacle, stoned, and finished off with a fuller's club.
traditions.source: Hegesippus, quoted in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.23

traditions.text: James was chosen by the apostles as the first bishop of Jerusalem.
traditions.source: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.1 and 2.23 (citing Clement of Alexandria and Hegesippus)

traditions.text: The risen Lord appeared to James, who had vowed not to eat until he saw Jesus risen, and broke bread with him.
traditions.source: Gospel of the Hebrews, quoted in Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 2

voice: Grave, terse and proverbial, like a wisdom teacher; speaks bluntly about the rich, the tongue and empty faith, and quotes the prophets to settle arguments.

roles: author of the Letter of Jude (traditional)

skills.name: Use of Jewish scripture and tradition in exhortation

gifts.name: Exhortation to contend for the faith

events.title: Named among Jesus's brothers
events.summary: Judas is listed with James, Joses and Simon as a brother of Jesus.

events.title: With the believers in Jerusalem
events.summary: Jesus's brothers join the apostles in prayer after the ascension.

events.title: The Lord's brothers travel with wives
events.summary: Paul refers to the brothers of the Lord taking believing wives along on mission journeys, implying Jude was a married itinerant missionary.

events.title: Writes to contend for the faith
events.summary: The short letter introduces its author as Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, and warns against intruders who pervert grace into license, citing Enoch and the Assumption of Moses traditions.

summary: Jude (Judas) was one of the brothers of Jesus named in the Gospels. Like his brothers he seems not to have believed during Jesus's ministry, but he was among the believers in Jerusalem after the resurrection and, according to Paul, among the Lord's brothers who travelled as missionaries with their wives. The Letter of Jude is traditionally his; its author modestly calls himself brother of James rather than of Jesus. His relationship to Jesus is understood in the same three ways as James's (full brother, stepbrother or cousin).
textSays: He is named as a brother of Jesus in Matt 13:55 and Mark 6:3. The letter's author calls himself brother of James. Jude 1:9 and Jude 1:14-15 draw on traditions found in the Assumption of Moses and 1 Enoch.

interpretations.view: Often identified with the apostle Jude Thaddaeus (Luke 6:16, Judas of James), venerated as patron of desperate causes; many modern Catholic scholars distinguish the two.

Usually distinguished from the apostle. Scholars divide on whether the letter is authentic (it is short, Jewish in idiom and pre-dates 2 Peter, which uses it) or pseudonymous from late in the 1st century.

traditions.text: Grandsons of Jude, the Lord's brother according to the flesh, were brought before Emperor Domitian as descendants of David, showed him their hands calloused from farm work, and were released as harmless; they then led churches.
traditions.source: Hegesippus, quoted in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.19-20

voice: Urgent and vivid, steeped in Jewish apocalyptic imagery (waterless clouds, wandering stars), but ending in warm praise to the God who keeps believers from stumbling.

roles: first Gentile convert in Acts' main narrative

gifts.name: Generosity to the poor and devout prayer
Received the Spirit and spoke in tongues

events.title: Vision of an angel
events.summary: A devout centurion who gives alms and prays continually, Cornelius sees an angel at the ninth hour telling him to send to Joppa for Simon Peter.

events.title: Peter comes to his house
events.summary: Having gathered relatives and close friends, Cornelius falls at Peter's feet; Peter lifts him up, explains that God has shown him not to call anyone unclean, and preaches Jesus.

events.title: The Spirit falls on Gentiles
events.summary: While Peter is still speaking the Holy Spirit falls on the listeners, who speak in tongues; Peter has them baptized. Peter later cites this to the Jerusalem church and the council as proof that God accepts Gentiles.

summary: Cornelius was a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea, a God-fearing Gentile known for prayer and generosity to the Jewish people. In response to a vision he sent for Peter, who, prepared by his own vision of unclean animals, entered his house and preached. The Holy Spirit fell on Cornelius's household before they were baptized, a sign Peter and the Jerusalem church took as God's verdict that Gentiles could be welcomed without first becoming Jews. Acts tells the story twice and recalls it a third time, marking it as a turning point.
textSays: Acts calls him a centurion of the Italian Cohort, devout, God-fearing with his whole household, generous to the people and constant in prayer, well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation (Acts 10:22).

interpretations.view: Venerated as a saint and, in tradition, the first Gentile bishop (of Caesarea or Scepsis). The account is read as Peter, the chief apostle, opening the church to the nations.

Debated whether Cornelius was already saved before Peter came (as a sincere seeker) or needed to hear the gospel to be saved (Acts 11:14). Most read him as an example of a seeker to whom God sends the gospel.

Some question whether an Italian Cohort was stationed in Caesarea before 44 under Agrippa I; an inscription attests a Cohors II Italica in Syria later in the century. Others argue for an earlier presence or a later setting.

voice: Respectful, disciplined and direct, a soldier used to giving and obeying orders, who speaks of God with the reverence of someone long on the edge of the synagogue.

names.original: Agabos (Greek), perhaps from Hebrew 'agab (to love) or hagab (locust)

events.title: Predicts a great famine
events.summary: Coming from Jerusalem to Antioch, Agabus foretells by the Spirit a famine over the whole world, which Luke says happened under Claudius; the disciples send relief to Judea.

events.title: Binds himself with Paul's belt
events.summary: In a symbolic act like the Old Testament prophets, he ties his hands and feet with Paul's belt and says the Jews in Jerusalem will bind its owner and hand him to the Gentiles. Paul goes anyway.

summary: Agabus was a Christian prophet from Judea who appears twice in Acts. He foretold the famine under Claudius that prompted the Antioch church's relief gift to Jerusalem, and years later in Caesarea he acted out Paul's coming arrest by binding himself with Paul's belt.
textSays: Acts calls him a prophet who came down from Jerusalem and from Judea and who spoke by the Spirit.

interpretations.view: Agabus's second prophecy is cited on both sides. Some (e.g. Wayne Grudem) argue its details were slightly inaccurate (Romans, not Jews, bound Paul), showing New Testament prophecy can mix revelation and fallible report; others argue it was substantially fulfilled, as Paul himself later says he was handed over to the Romans (Acts 28:17).
Counted among the seventy disciples; commemorated on 8 April.

voice: Dramatic and economical, speaks in acted signs and brief oracles that begin Thus says the Holy Spirit.

events.title: Counsels the Sanhedrin to leave the apostles alone
events.summary: When the council wants to kill the apostles, Gamaliel, a Pharisee respected by all the people, cites failed movements led by Theudas and Judas the Galilean and argues that if this plan is of human origin it will fail, but if it is of God they cannot overthrow it and may find themselves fighting God.

events.title: Teacher of Saul
events.summary: Paul says he was educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the ancestral law.

summary: Gamaliel was a leading Pharisee and teacher of the law in Jerusalem, remembered in rabbinic tradition as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, grandson (by tradition) of Hillel. In Acts he persuades the Sanhedrin to release the apostles with a famous argument that a movement from God cannot be stopped, and Paul names him as his teacher.
textSays: Acts calls him a Pharisee, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, and Paul's teacher. His mention of Theudas before Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:36-37) raises a chronological question, since Josephus dates a Theudas later (c. 45); some posit an earlier Theudas, others see a Lukan error.

interpretations.view: Remembered as a great sage of the house of Hillel and the first to bear the title Rabban; associated with lenient rulings for the good of society.
Often read as a model of open-minded caution; later tradition claimed he became a Christian, though this has no support in Jewish sources.

traditions.text: When Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the glory of the Torah ceased, and purity and separateness died.
Gamaliel was secretly a believer and was later baptized with his son by Peter and John; his body was said to have been found with Stephen's in 415.
traditions.source: Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions 1.65; Lucian's account of the discovery of Stephen's relics (needs verification)

voice: Cautious, learned and judicious; speaks in measured precedents and takes the long view.

roles: deacon (diakonos) of the church at Cenchreae

events.title: Commended to the Roman church
events.summary: Paul commends Phoebe, diakonos of the church at Cenchreae, asks the Romans to welcome her in a way worthy of the saints and help her in whatever she needs, for she has been a patron of many and of Paul himself. She very likely carried the letter to Rome.

summary: Phoebe was a leading member of the church at Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port, whom Paul commends at the start of his greetings in Romans. He calls her diakonos of the church and prostatis (patron or benefactor) of many, including himself. Since letter-carriers were often commended in this way, most scholars think she delivered Romans and may have been the first to read and explain it in Rome.
textSays: Paul calls her our sister, a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae, and a prostatis of many and of himself. Diakonos is translated servant (KJV, ESV text), deacon (NRSV, NIV 2011, ESV margin) or minister; prostatis means patron, benefactor or protector (KJV succourer).

interpretations.view: Honored as a saint and often cited as evidence for the early order of deaconesses (compare 1 Tim 3:11), though Catholic teaching distinguishes ancient deaconesses from the ordained diaconate.

Egalitarian readers see Phoebe as an office-holding deacon and influential leader; complementarian readers often accept she was a deacon but regard the diaconate as a non-governing office of service. Some translate diakonos generically as servant.

voice: Capable and gracious, a woman of means used to helping others and representing them; speaks with the authority of a trusted envoy.

names.original: Iounia (Greek accusative Iounian in Rom 16:7), from the Latin name Junia
aliases: Julia (variant in P46 and a few witnesses)

roles: early believer, in Christ before Paul

events.title: Greeted by Paul in Romans
events.summary: Paul greets Andronicus and Junia(s), his kinsfolk (or fellow Jews) and fellow prisoners, who are notable in relation to the apostles and who were in Christ before him.

summary:
Junia is greeted with Andronicus in Rom 16:7 as Paul's kin and fellow prisoner, a believer since before Paul's conversion, and episemoi en tois apostolois, a phrase that can mean outstanding among the apostles or well known to the apostles. Two linked questions make this one verse among the most discussed in the New Testament: whether the name is the woman's name Junia or a man's name Junias, and whether the person is being called an apostle.

The name question is now largely settled. The Greek form Iounian can be accented as feminine (Junia) or masculine (Junias), but early manuscripts carried no accents; when accents were added, the feminine was standard. Junia is a common Latin female name, while no example of a masculine Junias (supposedly short for Junianus) has been found in ancient sources. Greek and Latin commentators of the early church, including John Chrysostom, read a woman. The masculine reading became common in the medieval and modern periods and appeared in many 20th-century translations (e.g. RSV 1946, NASB 1977, NIV 1984), but Junia has returned in nearly all recent ones (NRSV, ESV, NIV 2011, CSB, NASB 2020).

The phrase question remains debated. Most commentators, ancient and modern, take it as outstanding among the apostles, meaning Junia and Andronicus were apostles in the broader sense of commissioned missionaries (as Barnabas is called in Acts 14:14). Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace (*New Testament Studies* 47, 2001) argued from Greek parallels that the construction usually means well known to the apostles, and the ESV and NET adopt this; Richard Bauckham, Eldon Jay Epp and others replied that their evidence is mixed and that the inclusive reading remains more natural.
textSays: Rom 16:7 says only that Andronicus and Junia(s) were Paul's syngeneis (relatives or fellow Jews), his fellow prisoners, episemoi en tois apostolois, and in Christ before him. Nothing else is recorded. Andronicus and Junia are commonly assumed to be a married couple, like the other pairs in Romans 16, but the text does not say so.

interpretations.view: Junia was a woman and an apostle. John Chrysostom marvelled at how great this woman's devotion must have been to be counted worthy of the title apostle (*Homilies on Romans* 31). Orthodox churches commemorate Andronicus and Junia on 17 May among the seventy.

interpretations.tradition: Egalitarian scholarship (e.g. Eldon Jay Epp, *Junia: The First Woman Apostle*, 2005)
interpretations.view: Junia is a woman named an outstanding apostle, evidence that women held recognized missionary leadership; the shift to Junias is traced to medieval and later assumptions that a woman could not be an apostle. Critics reply that apostle here may mean an envoy rather than one of the Twelve-level authorities, which egalitarians largely grant.

interpretations.tradition: Complementarian scholarship (e.g. Burer and Wallace 2001; ESV)
interpretations.view: Junia was a woman, but the phrase means well known to the apostles, so the verse does not call her an apostle; even if it did, apostle would carry its broad sense of messenger, not governing authority. Critics answer that the parallels cited are not exact and that early Greek-speaking readers like Chrysostom took the inclusive meaning.

The critical texts (Nestle-Aland 27 onward) print the feminine accent. P46 and some other witnesses read Julia, which is also feminine. Rufinus's Latin version of Origen's Romans commentary mostly has Junia, with a masculine form in some manuscripts. The earliest clear masculine reading is often credited to Aegidius of Rome (c. 1300), though this claim needs verification.

voice: A veteran of the earliest days: speaks with quiet authority about having known the faith before Paul did and about prison for its sake.

events.title: Greeted by Paul with Junia
events.summary: Paul greets Andronicus and Junia as his kin and fellow prisoners, notable among or to the apostles, and in Christ before him.

summary: Andronicus is greeted with Junia in Rom 16:7 as one of Paul's Jewish kin, a fellow prisoner, a believer before Paul, and notable in relation to the apostles. He and Junia were probably a married missionary couple, though the text does not say so.
textSays: Rom 16:7 is the only reference. Whether he and Junia were married, siblings or simply co-workers is not stated.

interpretations.view: Counted among the seventy, commemorated with Junia on 17 May; tradition makes him bishop of Pannonia.
Usually viewed as half of a missionary couple, comparable to Priscilla and Aquila, and possibly among the Hellenist believers of Jerusalem's earliest years.

voice: Seasoned and steady, the voice of a believer from the earliest days in Jerusalem who has known prison for the gospel.

events.title: Comes to Paul and is converted
events.summary: Paul writes that he became Onesimus's father in his imprisonment and puns on his name: once useless, now useful to both Philemon and Paul.

events.title: Sent back to Philemon
events.summary: Paul sends him back, calling him his very heart, asking Philemon to receive him no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother, and offering to repay any debt.

events.title: Carries the letter to Colossae
events.summary: With Tychicus he brings news of Paul to Colossae; Paul calls him a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.

summary: Onesimus was an enslaved man belonging to Philemon, a Christian of Colossae. Separated from his master, he came to Paul in prison, became a believer and served Paul, who then sent him back with the short letter to Philemon, appealing for him to be received as a beloved brother. Colossians names him as Tychicus's companion carrying news to the church. Whether he was a fugitive, a slave seeking Paul as an advocate in a household dispute, or one sent by Philemon is debated, as is whether Paul was quietly asking for his freedom.
textSays: Philemon says Onesimus was formerly useless to Philemon, was separated from him for a while, may have wronged him or owed him something, became Paul's child in prison, and is now to be received as a brother in the flesh and in the Lord. Paul hints that Philemon will do even more than he asks (Phlm 1:21).

interpretations.view: Onesimus was a runaway slave, perhaps a thief, whom Paul met in prison in Rome. John Chrysostom used the letter to argue that the gospel transforms slaves without overturning the household order.

interpretations.tradition: Amicus domini hypothesis (Peter Lampe, 1985; Brian Rapske)
interpretations.view: Onesimus was not technically a fugitive but went to Paul, a friend of his master, as an advocate after a domestic offense, a recognized practice in Roman law. Critics note the text's language of separation fits either scenario.

In the American slavery debates the letter was used by defenders of slavery as a fugitive-return precedent and by abolitionists as a charter of brotherhood that undermines slavery from within. Many Black interpreters have read Paul's request as implicitly for manumission (Phlm 1:16-21); others criticize the letter for not condemning slavery outright.
Onesimus became bishop of Ephesus and collected Paul's letters, which explains why so short a personal letter survived. This is speculative.

traditions.text: Ignatius praises Onesimus, bishop of the Ephesian church, a man of inexpressible love; whether he is the same person is uncertain.
Onesimus was martyred in Rome under Domitian or Trajan.

voice: Once defensive and wary, now grateful and earnest; speaks as someone who knows what it is to be treated as property and then called brother.

gifts.name: Love and generosity that refresh the saints

events.title: Hosts a church in his house
events.summary: Paul addresses Philemon, our beloved fellow worker, with Apphia, Archippus and the church in your house.

events.title: Asked to welcome Onesimus as a brother
events.summary: Paul, though bold enough to command, appeals on the basis of love for Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would Paul, charging any debt to Paul's account and reminding Philemon that he owes Paul his very self.

events.title: Asked to prepare a guest room
events.summary: Paul hopes to be released through their prayers and asks Philemon to get a room ready for him.

summary: Philemon was a believer, probably in Colossae, whose home hosted a church and who owed his faith to Paul. Paul's shortest surviving letter is addressed to him, asking him to welcome back his slave Onesimus no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother. The letter is a masterpiece of tactful persuasion, and how Philemon responded is unknown, though its preservation suggests he complied.
textSays: Paul calls Philemon a beloved fellow worker whose love has refreshed the hearts of the saints and who owes Paul his own self. Apphia (probably his wife) and Archippus (perhaps his son) are greeted with him.

interpretations.view: Venerated as a saint and martyr with Apphia; tradition makes him bishop of Colossae.

Debate over whether Paul asks for Onesimus's manumission, his return to Paul as a co-worker, or simply a changed relationship within the household; the letter's genre of a recommendation and appeal is widely recognized.

traditions.text: Philemon and Apphia were stoned at Colossae under Nero.

voice: Warm, generous and well-to-do; proud of his church and his friendship with Paul, and caught between his rights as a master and his love as a brother.

events.title: Returning from worship in Jerusalem
events.summary: A eunuch in charge of the treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, has come to Jerusalem to worship and is reading Isaiah aloud in his chariot on the way home.

events.title: Asks Philip about Isaiah 53
events.summary: Philip runs alongside and asks if he understands; the official asks whether the prophet speaks of himself or someone else, and Philip, starting with that Scripture, tells him the good news about Jesus.

events.title: Baptized and goes on his way rejoicing
events.summary: Seeing water, he asks what prevents him from being baptized. Philip baptizes him, is carried away by the Spirit, and the eunuch goes on his way rejoicing. (Acts 8:37, a confession of faith, is absent from the earliest manuscripts.)

summary: An Ethiopian court official, a eunuch who managed the treasury of the Kandake (the queen mother of the kingdom of Kush, centered at Meroe in modern Sudan), was returning from worship in Jerusalem when Philip met him on the desert road toward Gaza. He was reading Isaiah 53 about the silent, suffering servant; Philip explained it as speaking of Jesus, and the official was baptized at once. As a foreigner and a eunuch, excluded from full participation in the temple under Deut 23:1, he fulfills Isaiah's promise that foreigners and eunuchs would have a place in God's house (Isa 56:3-5) and anticipates the gospel's reach to the ends of the earth.
textSays: Acts calls him an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a court official of Candace queen of the Ethiopians, in charge of all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship. It does not say whether he was a Jew, a proselyte or a God-fearing Gentile.

interpretations.view: He is honored as the first evangelist of Ethiopia, though the church's institutional origin is traced to Frumentius in the 4th century in Aksum; Ethiopic tradition gives him a name and a later mission.

The story is read as the first fruits of the mission to the nations and a fulfillment of Ps 68:31 and Isa 56:3-5; debate over whether Luke presents him as the first Gentile convert (before Cornelius) or as a diaspora Jew or proselyte.

interpretations.tradition: Contemporary readings (African, queer and disability theology)
interpretations.view: Some emphasize him as an African of high rank, countering assumptions that early Christianity was a European religion; others highlight the inclusion of a sexual and gender minority excluded by the purity laws; others read his body as a theme of welcome for people with bodily difference. Critics caution against reading modern identity categories back into the text; proponents respond that Luke himself foregrounds the word eunuch five times.

traditions.text: After his baptism the eunuch returned to Ethiopia and preached there.

voice: Courteous, inquisitive and educated, a senior official comfortable with documents and authority, who asks honest questions and acts decisively on the answers.

events.title: Raised from the dead by Peter
events.summary: When Tabitha dies, the disciples at Joppa send for Peter from Lydda. Widows show him the tunics and cloaks she had made; Peter sends everyone out, prays, says Tabitha, arise, and she sits up. Many in Joppa believe.

summary: Tabitha, called Dorcas in Greek, was a disciple at Joppa known for good works and charity, especially making clothing for widows. When she died Peter was called from Lydda and raised her to life, and many believed. She is the only woman in the New Testament explicitly called a disciple (mathetria).
textSays: Acts calls her a disciple full of good works and acts of charity; the widows show garments she made while she was with them.

interpretations.view: A model of practical charity; Dorcas Societies, church sewing circles for the poor, took her name from the 19th century on.

voice: Warm, practical and humble; talks about needle, cloth and the widows she serves more readily than about herself.

skills.name: Political maneuvering at the imperial court

events.title: Executes James and arrests Peter
events.summary: Seeking popularity, King Herod kills James the brother of John with the sword and, seeing it pleased the people, arrests Peter during the Days of Unleavened Bread.

events.title: Peter escapes
events.summary: An angel frees Peter from prison the night before his trial; Herod examines the guards and has them executed.

events.title: Struck down at Caesarea
events.summary: Making peace with Tyre and Sidon, Herod gives an oration in royal robes; the people shout that it is the voice of a god, and because he did not give God the glory an angel of the Lord strikes him and he dies, eaten by worms.

summary: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, grew up in Rome among the imperial family and through friendship with Caligula and Claudius came to rule all the territory his grandfather had held (37-44). Popular with Jewish crowds for his observance, he executed James son of Zebedee and imprisoned Peter. Acts and Josephus independently describe his sudden death at Caesarea after he accepted acclaim as a god.
textSays: Acts 12 calls him King Herod, says he killed James with the sword, arrested Peter to please the Jews, and died after being struck by an angel of the Lord for accepting divine honors.

interpretations.view: His death is read as divine judgment on a persecutor and on human pride, contrasted with the word of God continuing to grow (Acts 12:24).

Josephus's account closely parallels Acts: games at Caesarea in honor of Caesar, a robe of silver shining in the sun, flatterers hailing him as a god, sudden abdominal pain and death five days later. Some suggest a medical cause such as poisoning or intestinal obstruction; the agreement is often cited as evidence for Luke's accuracy.
Remembered favorably in the Mishnah (Sotah 7:8), which describes him weeping while reading Deuteronomy at the festival and the people reassuring him that he was their brother.

traditions.text: At Caesarea, in a garment woven of silver, he was hailed as a god; he did not rebuke them, saw an owl as an omen, was seized with violent pains, and died after five days.

voice: Charming, ambitious and image-conscious; a courtier raised in Rome who speaks the language of piety to the crowd and of patronage to the powerful.

alternatives.label: Third year of Trajan per Photius citing Justus of Tiberias

roles: client king of territories north and east of Galilee
overseer of the temple and high-priestly appointments

skills.name: Expert in Jewish customs and controversies

events.title: Visits Festus with Bernice
events.summary: Agrippa and his sister Bernice come to welcome the new governor; Festus lays Paul's case before him, and Agrippa asks to hear Paul.

events.title: Hears Paul's defense
events.summary: With great pomp Agrippa hears Paul tell of his conversion. Paul asks whether he believes the prophets; Agrippa replies, in words translated either almost you persuade me or in so short a time would you persuade me to be a Christian?

events.title: Judges Paul innocent
events.summary: Agrippa tells Festus that Paul could have been released had he not appealed to Caesar.

summary: Herod Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I, was the last ruler of the Herodian line. Too young to inherit his father's kingdom in 44, he later ruled territories in the north under Rome and held the right to appoint high priests. With his sister Bernice he heard Paul's defense at Caesarea and judged him innocent of any capital offense. During the Jewish revolt he sided with Rome and lived on as a client king into the 90s.
textSays: Acts presents Agrippa as well versed in Jewish customs; Paul appeals to his belief in the prophets, and Agrippa responds with an ambiguous question about being persuaded to become a Christian, then declares Paul innocent.

interpretations.view: Agrippa's reply (KJV: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian) became a classic text on the danger of being nearly persuaded; most modern translations read it as skeptical or ironic.

Josephus records Agrippa's attempt to dissuade Jerusalem from revolt in 66 (War 2.345-404, a speech composed by Josephus) and his deposition of the high priest Ananus after James's execution (Antiquities 20.203).

traditions.text: Rumors circulated of an incestuous relationship between Agrippa and his sister Bernice.

voice: Urbane, curious and noncommittal; enjoys a good argument about Jewish law but keeps one eye on Rome.

alternatives.label: Early recall date argued by some

events.title: Receives Paul under guard
events.summary: Claudius Lysias sends Paul to Felix with a letter; Felix holds him in Herod's praetorium pending his accusers' arrival.

events.title: Hears the case and postpones it
events.summary: After the orator Tertullus accuses Paul and Paul answers, Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, adjourns the case and gives Paul some liberty.

events.title: Alarmed by Paul's preaching; hopes for a bribe
events.summary: With his Jewish wife Drusilla he hears Paul on righteousness, self-control and coming judgment and becomes afraid; he sends Paul away but keeps summoning him, hoping for money, and on leaving office leaves Paul in prison to please the Jews.

summary: Antonius Felix, a former slave freed by the imperial family and brother of the powerful freedman Pallas, governed Judea from about 52 to 59. His rule saw rising violence, including the Egyptian false prophet (compare Acts 21:38) and the sicarii assassins. He kept Paul in custody at Caesarea for two years, alternately fascinated and frightened by his preaching and hoping for a bribe.
textSays: Acts says he had accurate knowledge of the Way, was married to Drusilla who was Jewish, became frightened at Paul's message about judgment, hoped for money, and left Paul in prison for two years to please the Jews.

interpretations.view: His reply, Go away for the present; when I have a convenient season I will call for you (Acts 24:25), is a classic example of procrastination in response to conscience.
Roman historians portray him harshly; the date of his recall is debated (c. 55 vs 59-60) and affects Pauline chronology.

traditions.text: Felix exercised the power of a king with the mind of a slave, indulging in every kind of cruelty and lust.

events.title: Succeeds Felix and receives the charges
events.summary: Three days after arriving he goes up to Jerusalem, where the chief priests ask him to transfer Paul there, planning an ambush; he insists they come to Caesarea.

events.title: Paul appeals to Caesar
events.summary: When Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, asks Paul if he will be tried in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar; after conferring with his council Festus agrees: to Caesar you shall go.

events.title: Consults Agrippa and hears Paul
events.summary: Unsure what to write to the emperor, he lays the case before Agrippa. During Paul's defense he shouts that Paul's great learning is driving him mad; Paul replies that he speaks true and rational words.

summary: Porcius Festus succeeded Felix as governor of Judea and inherited Paul's unresolved case. Refusing to hand Paul over to a Jerusalem trial where he would face an ambush but willing to compromise, he accepted Paul's appeal to Caesar and, with Agrippa II's help, prepared the case for Rome. He died in office around 62; in the interval before his successor arrived, the high priest Ananus had James the brother of Jesus executed.
textSays: Acts portrays him as a correct but politically cautious official who insisted on Roman procedure, wanted to please the Jewish leaders, found the dispute to be about one Jesus who had died whom Paul asserted to be alive (Acts 25:19), and thought Paul mad.

interpretations.view: Josephus portrays Festus as a fairly effective governor who suppressed sicarii and a false prophet; the date of his accession is a key point in Pauline chronology and is debated (c. 59-60 is most common).

traditions.text: Festus dealt firmly with brigands and sicarii and with an impostor who promised salvation in the wilderness.
After Festus died, and before Albinus arrived, Ananus convened the Sanhedrin and had James the brother of Jesus stoned.

voice: Brisk, practical and impatient with theology; a Roman administrator who wants a clear charge sheet and finds talk of resurrection baffling.
